summary.text: The celestial sphere is an abstract sphere of arbitrarily large radius, concentric to Earth, onto which all objects in the sky can be imagined as projected.
Astronomers use it to specify an object's position in the sky without considering how far away the object is.
Remote objects reveal nothing about their real distances, so they all seem equally far away, as if fixed to a sphere that appears to rotate westward overhead.

facts.label: Equator
facts.value: The celestial equator divides it into northern and southern hemispheres

facts.label: Infinite radius
facts.value: It can be treated as infinite, so any point can be the center

facts.label: Parallax effect
facts.value: Nearby objects like the Moon appear to shift as the observer moves

facts.label: Sphere counts
facts.value: Eudoxus modelled 27 spheres in the heavens; Aristotle modelled 55

items.prompt: You look up at a clear night sky. Why do the stars all seem equally far away?

options.label: They really are all fixed at the same distance
Earth's air makes distant stars appear nearer
Their distances are so great that looking gives no sign of them
Brighter stars are always closer than dim ones

items.explain: Because astronomical objects are at such remote distances, casual observation offers no information on their actual distances.

items.prompt: Two observers on opposite sides of Earth see the Moon at slightly different spots against the distant stars. What is this effect called?

options.label: Parallax
Precession
Retrogression
Refraction

items.explain: Relatively near objects such as the Moon seem to change position against the distant celestial sphere if the observer moves far enough; this is parallax.

items.prompt: Astronomers want to split the sky's imaginary sphere into northern and southern halves. What do they use?

options.label: The celestial pole
The sublunary line
The vanishing circle
The celestial equator

items.explain: The celestial equator divides the celestial sphere into northern and southern hemispheres.

items.prompt: An astronomer wants positions as they would look from the Sun's center, not Earth's. Is that allowed?

options.label: No, it must always be centered on the observer
Yes, the sphere can be centered anywhere convenient
No, it must always be centered on Earth's center
Yes, but only for objects closer than the Moon

items.explain: The celestial sphere can be considered to be centered at the Earth's center, the Sun's center, or any other convenient location.

items.prompt: Does it matter for spherical astronomy whether the sky really turns or Earth turns beneath it?

options.label: No, since it deals only with directions to objects
Yes, since the sphere's radius depends on it
Yes, since distances must be known first
No, since the sphere is known to be still

items.explain: Spherical astronomy is concerned only with the directions to celestial objects, so it makes no difference which one rotates.

items.prompt: In Aristotle's geocentric model, where did the perfect, incorruptible bodies lie?

options.label: In the sublunary region, below the Moon's sphere
In the same region as fire, water, air and earth
In the superlunary region, above the sublunary sphere
In a region that was spread evenly throughout

items.explain: Corruptible elements were contained only in the sublunary region, and incorruptible elements were in the superlunary region.
